Proclamation Society
prok-lə-mā'shən sə-sī'ə-tee
n. (the society founded by William Wilberforce in 1787 to enforce the royal proclamation against vice and immorality)
Latin proclamatio, a crying out; societas, fellowship.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Proclamation Society was Wilberforce's second great cause. In the same year that he wrote in his journal that God had set before him two great objects, the suppression of the slave trade and the reformation of manners, he persuaded the Archbishop of Canterbury and others to obtain from George III a royal Proclamation for the Encouragement of Piety and Virtue, and for the Preventing and Punishing of Vice, Profaneness, and Immorality, issued on 1 June 1787. Wilberforce then organized a society of bishops, peers, and magistrates to see that the proclamation was enforced, urging local justices to act against drunkenness, Sabbath-breaking, blasphemy, gambling houses, and the sale of obscene publications. In 1797 the society brought the prosecution of Thomas Williams for publishing Thomas Paine's Age of Reason. In 1802 its work passed to the more vigorous Society for the Suppression of Vice. Critics mocked it as a scheme to police the pleasures of the poor while sparing the rich; Wilberforce's answer was that the example must begin at the top, and that a nation's laws teach as well as restrain. His conviction was the proverb's: “Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people” (Pro 14:34).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a proclamation as an official public notice given by the supreme authority, and vice as any voluntary action contrary to the moral law.

expand to see more

PROCLAMA'TION, n. Official notice given to the public; an official public notice given by the supreme executive of a kingdom or state.

VICE, n. In ethics, any voluntary action or course of conduct which deviates from the rules of moral rectitude, or from the plain rules of propriety.

PROFANE'NESS, n. Irreverence of sacred things; particularly, the use of language which implies irreverence towards God.

Key Scripture

Pro 14:34 — "Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people."

Rom 13:3 — "For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same:"

1Ti 2:2 — "For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty."

Eph 5:11 — "And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them."

Modern Corruption

Wilberforce's campaign for the reformation of manners under royal proclamation.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Modern readers find the Proclamation Society embarrassing, a puritanical intrusion that sits awkwardly beside the abolition campaign. Wilberforce saw no such division. The magistrate who protects the slave and the magistrate who restrains public vice are the same minister of God, of whom Paul says “rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil” (Rom 13:3).

The honest caveat is the critics' own: law that falls hardest on the poor while the fashionable sin in comfort is not righteousness but respectability. The principle to recover is that the church's first weapon against vice is not the constable but reproof and example: “have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them” (Eph 5:11).

Usage

"“sin is a reproach to any people” (Pro 14:34) — the case for reformation of manners."

"“not a terror to good works, but to the evil” (Rom 13:3) — the magistrate's office."

"“but rather reprove them” (Eph 5:11) — the church's part."
